findings.title: manifest._version_of() can never read a real version token for object-storage runs, so catchments()/catchment_group()/crosswalk() cache stale sidecar data forever
findings.why_it_matters: catchments(), catchment_group() and crosswalk() key their lru_cache on (run_path, _version_of(run_path)). _version_of() calls manifest.read(run_path), which builds the manifest path with os.path.join and opens it with the builtin open(). When object storage is configured, run_path is an s3://bucket/prefix/name URI (run_store.location()/entry['path']), and open() cannot resolve that string -- it raises FileNotFoundError, which read() catches and turns into None, so _version_of() always returns ''. run_store.py's own docstring for _read_manifest already documents this exact limitation of manifest.read() ('manifest.read opens a filesystem path, which does not exist in a bucket') but the fix was applied only to the run listing, not to these three sidecar accessors that utils.py calls with entry['path'] on every catchment/crosswalk read. Net effect: the very first read for a run populates the cache under key (path, ''); if that run is later deleted and a different run is published under the same name (ingest.publish's own duplicate-name check forces exactly this delete-then-reupload flow), or an operator reruns write_manifest/convert_outputs on a live S3-backed run, any long-running worker process that already touched the old run keeps serving its old catchment membership and flowpath crosswalk under the identical cache key, indefinitely, with no error. Contrast with RunOutputs.version, _cached_troute_frame, _cached_catchment_variables and _cached_value_matrix in utils.py, which correctly thread version_token from the already-loaded (storage-aware) manifest document instead of re-deriving it -- only these three manifest.py accessors have the bug.
findings.suggested_fix: Let catchments()/catchment_group()/crosswalk() accept the version_token from the caller (utils.py already has it on the loaded manifest document, e.g. entry['manifest']['version_token'] / RunOutputs.version) instead of recomputing it via _version_of()/read(). Fall back to _version_of() only for call sites that genuinely have no document (e.g. write_manifest.py, backfill_manifests.py, which only ever pass local paths anyway).

findings.title: ensure_superuser does not refuse a hosted start when no superuser credentials are supplied at all, leaving the baked admin/pass account live
findings.why_it_matters: The module docstring and README both state a hosted deployment 'refuses to start' on the image's baked admin/pass account. _refuse_shipped_defaults() only raises when the *supplied* PORTAL_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD literally equals BAKED_PASSWORD ('pass'). If PORTAL_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD is simply unset (the empty-string default from os.environ.get), the comparison '' == 'pass' is False, so hosted=True passes the check silently (--check-only even prints 'no shipped defaults in use'). Execution then falls through to `if not name or not password: ... leaving the database alone`, which returns without touching the database -- so the build-time admin/pass superuser, created into the image and restored on every restart of an ephemeral hosted database, remains fully live and undetected. This is the same class of bug the command exists to prevent, just triggered by omission instead of by explicitly re-entering the default. test_write_auth.py only exercises the no-credentials path under the 'local' fixture, never under 'hosted'.
findings.suggested_fix: In hosted mode, treat a missing password (and/or missing name) the same as the baked-default case: e.g. in _refuse_shipped_defaults, or right after it, add `if hosted and not password: problems.append("PORTAL_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD is not set, so the image's baked admin/pass account would remain the only login.")` before the `if not name or not password: ... return` early-exit.

findings.title: The uploaded archive file is never deleted after ingest, leaking the full archive to local disk on every upload
findings.why_it_matters: ingest.publish(archive_path, ...) reads archive_path to extract it but never removes it; only the unpack workspace is cleaned up (`finally: shutil.rmtree(workspace, ...)` in ingest.py). ingest_archive.py's handle() computes `path = local_archive or self._staged(job_id)` and passes it straight to publish(); its own finally block only calls `ingest.discard_staged(job_id)`, which deletes the *object-storage* staging key, not this local file. Two upload paths therefore leak a full local copy of every uploaded archive forever: (1) controllers.uploadRun's direct-upload mode writes the browser's POST body to a `tempfile.mkstemp(..., suffix='.archive')` file that is passed as `--archive` and never removed; (2) the presigned S3 mode's `Command._staged()` downloads the staged object to another mkstemp file that is likewise never removed after publish. Given archives can be up to the 32 GiB unpacked-size ceiling (and are often multi-GB compressed), repeated uploads on a self-hosted deployment will steadily fill the local disk the portal runs on and eventually take the whole container down -- exactly the failure mode the module docstring for archive.py warns about for archive *expansion*, but here it is the raw upload itself that is never reclaimed. test_upload.py's `test_the_workspace_is_cleaned_up` only checks the `ngiab-ingest-*` workspace prefix, not the archive file.
findings.suggested_fix: In ingest_archive.py's handle(), remove the local archive file in the same finally block that already runs `ingest.discard_staged(job_id)`, e.g. `finally: os.path.exists(path) and os.remove(path)` (guard for the case where `_staged`/publish raised before `path` was assigned). This covers both the fetched-from-S3 temp file and the directly-uploaded temp file from controllers.uploadRun, since both flow through the same `path` variable.

findings.title: The manifest version_token ignores the t-route output directory, so re-converting t-route alone serves a stale cached troute frame
findings.why_it_matters: _version_token() hashes only output_dir's file names/sizes, the catchment count, and the gpkg's size -- it never looks at outputs/troute. utils.get_troute_df() caches the parsed troute frame in _cached_troute_frame keyed on (directory, document['version_token'], source, source_format). If a run's t-route output is regenerated in place (e.g. an operator reruns t-route with different routing parameters against the same, unchanged ngen outputs and the same GeoPackage) and convert_outputs/write_manifest is rerun, the manifest is rewritten but version_token comes out byte-identical because nothing that feeds the hash changed. Any process that already read the old troute file for that run keeps serving the previous readings under the same cache key, indefinitely -- the same failure mode the docstring for _version_token explicitly calls out for object storage ('leaving the cache key constant, so a re-ingested run would serve stale bins forever'), just triggered from the one directory the hash forgets to cover.
findings.suggested_fix: Fold the t-route directory's file names/sizes into the same digest, mirroring the loop already used for output_dir: `for name in sorted(os.listdir(_TROUTE_SUBDIR)) ...: digest.update(...)`, so a troute-only reconversion changes the token.

findings.title: Archive member-count cap is off by one, admitting max_members + 1 entries
findings.why_it_matters: In archive.inspect(), the `len(entries) > max_members` check runs before `entries.append(...)`, so it compares the pre-append length. When length reaches exactly max_members (500,000), the check is `500000 > 500000` (False), the member is still appended, and the loop only raises on the *next* member -- so an archive with 500,001 entries passes where the docstring/ceiling implies 500,000 is the limit. Low impact given how generous the default is, but it is a genuine boundary miss in a security-relevant guard (unbounded member counts are one of the three threats archive.py exists to stop).
findings.suggested_fix: Move the check after the append (`entries.append(...)` then `if len(entries) > max_members: raise`), or change the comparison to `len(entries) + 1 > max_members`.

residual_risks: Two uploads for the same run name racing each other can both pass the pre-flight `run_store.find(name) is None` check (once in createUpload's process, once again in the separate ingest_archive subprocess for each job) before either has published, then both reach ingest._publish_directory for the same run_name: on the local backend shutil.move onto an existing destination directory nests the second run's contents inside the first instead of failing; on S3 both writers save the same object keys, interleaving files from two different archives into one run. This needs concurrent identically-named uploads to trigger, which is why it is not filed as a standalone finding, but there is no lock or atomic rename step preventing it.
testing_gaps: No test calls manifest.catchments()/catchment_group()/crosswalk() with an s3:// run_path (the object_root fixture is only exercised against run_store.location()/duckdb_secret_sql(), not against these three manifest accessors), so the version-token cache defeat described above would not be caught by the current suite.

test_write_auth.py's ensure_superuser tests only exercise the 'no credentials supplied' path under the local fixture; there is no test for hosted mode with PORTAL_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD/NAME left unset, which is the case that silently boots with the baked admin/pass account.

test_upload.py's test_the_workspace_is_cleaned_up only asserts the ngiab-ingest-* workspace directory is removed; nothing asserts the archive file itself (uploaded temp file or fetched staged file) is cleaned up after a job completes.
